entry.summary:

Their peer-reviewed design does not permit a reputation score to execute access by itself because a resource owner first signs an attribute-based access policy. The distinction is material, but the result is not merely advisory reputation. The minimum trust and reputation scores form part of the access policy. entry.title: Answerability As Deployment Control
entry.summary:
Enterprise deployability is an institutional property that Horneber and Laumer classify across social, institutional, organizational, and technical accountability layers. Their central distinction is that a machine learning system, as a technical artifact, cannot itself be held accountable, while the organization and the people who develop, operate, or employ it remain the parties who must justify its design, use, and outcomes.
This distinction changes the deployment question. Technical reliability is relevant. It does not designate the actor who bears consequences, provides information, or satisfies external demands. entry.title: Attack Specific Reputation Design
entry.summary:
Threat resistance belongs inside the specification of a reputation system. Hoffman, Zage, and Nita-Rotaru decompose a reputation system into formulation, calculation, and dissemination components, classify attack classes, and use that decomposition to identify the design choices each attack exploits. This method links an attack class to a defense rather than treating a reputation score as self-validating.
Their survey identifies a specific composite mechanism. The attack is composite. One actor can acquire multiple identities and collude through them even when source data is authenticated. The colluding identities can participate mutually in events that generate real feedback at a rate that improves their scores faster than honest participation. entry.title: Contextual Outcomes Over Promotional Reputation
entry.summary:
Reputation is a selection mechanism. Gandhi, Hollenbeck, and Li study products that purchased fake reviews on Amazon and the honest products that competed with them, and their equilibrium simulations attribute a 27.2 percent increase in units sold to the manipulators and a 4.4 percent decline for honest products. entry.summary:
Revocation is a state problem. Chen and his coauthors compare Intel MPK, ARM PAC, ARM MTE, and ARM Morello capabilities. They find that rights retained in registers on other cores prevent a revoking core from establishing that the right has disappeared, unless the system uses an interprocessor interrupt or a restricted single core model. Of the four mechanisms, only MTE implements the core coherent synchronization principle they identify.

The issuer's record proves a local change. The prior right may remain live elsewhere. Local withdrawal is not cessation. Every live instance matters. entry.title: Delegation Chain Authority Intersection
entry.summary:
Authority can exceed consent even when the final permission check is correct. Felt and her coauthors identify permission redelegation where an application holding a user granted permission performs a privileged task for an application that lacks it. The system approves the call because the immediate deputy has the required permission. The requester nonetheless causes an action that it could not invoke directly. The paper reports fifteen such vulnerabilities across five core Android applications.
The mechanism supplies a concrete instance of authority drift. A user grants authority to one application. entry.title: Traceable Composition Responsibility
entry.summary:
Attribution is a system property, not a label added after failure. Kroll's account of traceability connects the provenance of components, design choices, and operation to specific outcomes and to the question of whom to hold responsible. He also draws a necessary boundary. A mechanical path from input to output does not explain why the system works as it does. Traceability depends on the system in use, its origins, and the decisions that produced its behavior.
That distinction is especially important when a workflow crosses independently operated components. A record that an authorized call occurred may identify the caller. It does not establish which component contributed to the harmful outcome, whether the component behaved within its assigned function, or which design and operational decisions made the outcome possible. entry.title: Four Accountability Failure Tests
entry.summary:
Accountability is not a single property of an agent runtime. Chappidi and her coauthors define an accountability relationship through an actor who owes an account, a forum entitled to receive it, and information that permits review and response. They then distinguish records from a system, which describe its operation, from records about a system, which describe how it was commissioned, built, deployed, and monitored. Records may support investigation, oversight, challenge, repair, and redress. The paper also identifies accountability capture. The apparatus used to observe conduct can reconfigure the conduct, induce evasion, and distort the accountability regime itself.

entry.title: Workflow Arrangement Amortization
entry.summary:
Scale is an amortization problem before it is a throughput problem. Chen and her coauthors make this distinction explicit in AgentSlimming. Their starting workflow is a graph of agents and communication edges. The method prunes redundant nodes, substitutes lower-cost models, and retains changes only when baseline performance survives. Across eight benchmarks, the resulting workflows reduced recurring token and API expense while preserving or improving selected task scores. The authors then separate the one-time search and evaluation burden from per-query inference savings and calculate time to break even.

entry.summary:

The model concerns human organizations, communication, and control. It does not measure responsibility, remedy, value attribution, security review, or agent integration. entry.title: Outcome Responsibility Allocation
entry.summary:
A crossing core can decide whether an agent may act. It cannot decide who should bear the consequences of a joint result merely by replaying an authorized call. Triantafyllou, Singla, and Radanovic formalize blame attribution in cooperative multi-agent sequential decision making as a separate allocation problem. Their comparison shows that the selected rule matters. Shapley value can fail performance monotonicity, Banzhaf allocation may over-blame, and more cautious methods sacrifice explanatory power. The same trace can therefore support materially different assignments of responsibility under different allocation rules.

entry.title: Integration Governance Settlement
entry.summary:
Technical interoperability does not settle an institutional relation. Swales, Gooden, and Thaldar reach the same boundary through a scoping review of twenty-four data transfer agreements. The agreements identify the parties, state the purpose of the transfer, allocate duties, restrict processing, provide for audit, assign liability, and specify termination and dispute resolution. These clauses do more than document an exchange. They determine who acts, what the recipient may do, how compliance is assessed, who bears loss, and what follows from breach. The evidence independently extends Kaal's claim: a new integration needs a governance settlement before data or authority crosses the boundary.

entry.title: Machine Speed Boundary Costs
entry.summary:
Digital coordination lowers a transaction cost. It does not eliminate the economic boundary that creates it. Baldwin and Robert-Nicoud model fragmented production as trade in tasks. Their framework assigns one cost to coordinating an offshore task within the firm and an additional nonnegative cost when a separate firm performs it. Advances in information and communication technology can lower both costs, but the effect varies by task. Routine, codifiable tasks may approach zero coordination cost, while complex tasks can remain too costly to move. The mechanism independently extends Kaal's claim: speed and automation can conceal the cross-boundary relation without converting it into an internal operation.

entry.title: Feature Counterparty Firm Boundary
entry.summary:
The boundary between a feature and a counterparty is not determined by technical integration alone. Alfaro and her coauthors show why ownership matters. Within firm boundaries, management can reassign control among integrated suppliers. Outside the firm, an independent supplier retains control through separate ownership. Non-integration has legal force, and reversal or dispute requires legal institutions between parties. The same mechanism applies when software crosses an economic boundary.
The evidence is narrower than Kaal's claim. The study examines firms, input suppliers, and production decisions rather than plugins or sovereign agent runtimes. It does not establish that every external service demands the same institutional form. It establishes the controlling classification. entry.title: Machine Settlement Institutional Boundary
entry.summary:
Machine settlement is not only a transport function. Athanassiou's analysis of automated payments shows why. Smart contracts can validate, execute, and record pre-agreed responses without human intermediation. Once value moves, however, the arrangement raises questions about contractual intent, counterparty identity, settlement finality, liability, and access to adjudication when code fails or parties dispute the result. Automation therefore changes the institutional classification of the system even when the transfer protocol remains technically sound.
The evidence is narrower than Kaal's claim. The ECB paper examines distributed ledgers, smart contracts, and retail payments rather than sovereign agent runtimes. entry.title: User Controlled Decryption Custody Test
entry.summary:
Encryption at rest does not establish user-held state when the service provider controls the keys. Hofmann and Truong show why. In their analysis of end-to-end encrypted cloud storage, provider-held keys supply no protection once the provider is compromised. The relevant alternative encrypts files under keys managed by the user and evaluates confidentiality against a server with full access to its own infrastructure. This moves custody from a promise about data location to a test of decryption authority.
The evidence is narrower than the general claim. The study concerns cloud storage, not agent working memory, and it documents flaws even in systems marketed as zero knowledge. User-managed keys can still fail through protocol defects, malicious client delivery, weak credentials, or metadata leakage. Those limits sharpen the classification. entry.summary:

Kleppmann and coauthors distinguish cloud applications from local-first software by the location of the primary data copy, the presence of a locally installed executable, and continued operation without a network connection. This independently extends Kaal's operational test: retained function under isolation supplies observable evidence that computation and state remain on the user's device.

That architecture independently supports the proposition that class membership should be tested against system properties rather than branding.

entry.title: Local Custody Workflow Provenance
entry.summary:
Custody is not an execution history. Kifor and coauthors study agent-mediated healthcare systems in which data, procedures, and logs are divided among heterogeneous autonomous information systems. They show that provenance-aware instrumentation can record events, dependencies, and human decisions across those systems. The resulting process documentation represents the distributed execution, connects its causal steps, and permits later reconstruction and audit. This independently extends Kaal's failure claim: custody identifies where the bytes reside, but a separate recording architecture must preserve what the composed services did.

entry.title: Sovereign Custody Institutional Accountability
entry.summary:
Cryptographic self-custody can secure operational sovereignty without supplying institutional accountability. Hu and Rong show that decentralized agents derive persistence and resistance to override from cryptographic keys, trusted execution environments, and distributed protocols. The same layered architecture diffuses responsibility across developers, infrastructure providers, protocol governance, and economic participants. Their analysis independently extends Kaal's distinction: control over custody identifies where assets sit and who can reach them, but does not identify who acted under authority or who answers for a harmful outcome.

entry.title: Finacial Decentralization And Local Self Governance In The Period Of Reforms 7184Bb96
entry.summary: Formal expenditure authority does not secure fiscal autonomy. Chernyavsky and Vartapetov report that Russian municipalities remained completely dependent on higher-level governments despite significant formal expenditure powers. This evidence extends Kaal's claim that local authority must be paired with control over adequate revenues. It does not establish that the same dependency arises in every decentralized system.

entry.title: Gpos Geospatially Aware Proof Of Stake 4C1A4F6B
entry.summary: GPoS: Geospatially-aware Proof of Stake reports a distinct concentration mechanism in proof-of-stake consensus. Across Aptos, Avalanche, Ethereum, Solana, and Sui, a few geographic regions dominate consensus voting power. The study reports limited geospatial decentralization and tests a geospatially aware voting design. Its experiments report a 45 percent average improvement in geospatial decentralization with minimal overhead in the tested BFT protocols. Kaal's claim that token-weighted proof-of-stake governance can concentrate control is extended along a geographic dimension. That extension does not validate the wealth-based mechanism. Only the Crossref-indexed abstract passed because the ACM PDF returned HTTP 403. Broader governance outcomes remain unverified.

entry.title: Blockchain Technologies Probability Of Double Spend Attack On A Proof Of Stake Consensus 4A40Bf47
entry.summary: Blockchain Technologies: Probability of Double-Spend Attack on a Proof-of-Stake Consensus quantifies two attack strategies. Their success probabilities depend on network parameters and confirmation depth. The authors use those results to derive the number of confirmations a vendor should await before delivering goods or services. These findings extend Kaal's claim that fixed consensus rules cannot eliminate strategic attacks by independent nodes. Transaction finality and confirmation depth bound, but do not remove, proof-of-stake double-spend risk. Only the Crossref-indexed abstract passed because the publisher PDF returned HTTP 403. No inference reaches every proof-of-stake protocol.

entry.title: Strategic Mining In Proof Of Stake With Practical Random Election 3E2Ce91D
entry.summary: Strategic Mining in Proof-of-Stake with Practical Random Election identifies a concrete failure in validator selection. Distributed random beacons fix randomness across several slots because of latency. Validators can infer future election information. The study reports that, without propagation delay, a validator with any proportion of stake can profit from strategic mining and obtain higher block rewards than prior strategies. The result extends Kaal's claim that fixed consensus rules remain vulnerable to strategic gaming as conditions change. It is limited to the modeled protocol and its no-delay assumption. The evidence does not establish failure across all proof-of-stake systems.

entry.title: Veritas Layer 2 Scaling Solution For Decentralized Oracles On Ethereum Blockchain With Rep Baa7239B
entry.summary: Oracles reveal an external-data boundary in smart contracts. Veritas examines a decentralized Ethereum oracle architecture for information that does not exist on chain. Simulation and experimental analysis reports lower operational costs. It also reports limited malicious data entry and preserved security. The architecture therefore extends Kaal's claim that a decentralized economy requires a trustworthy decentralized information layer, but the evidence remains limited to one Ethereum design. The result is consistent with a narrow mechanism, not a general rule. It does not establish a universal requirement for every news service. Nor does it prove that the node-selection process remains robust in production.

entry.title: Quantum Secure Blockchain And Decentralized Systems 6Ad36F49
entry.summary: Quantum computing creates a two-sided problem for blockchain cryptography. Quantum-Secure Blockchain and Decentralized Systems evaluates lattice-based, multivariate, and hash-based signatures, then reports simulation-based robustness against quantum-enabled attacks while preserving decentralization, transparency, and immutability. Those results extend Kaal's claim that blockchain security depends on quantum-resistant algorithms. The available evidence is limited to the abstract. Because the source is posted preprint content, it cannot independently establish production readiness or the claimed efficiency benefits of quantum computing.

entry.title: Dynamic Decentralized Reputation System From Blockchain And Secure Multiparty Computation Dd0930F4
entry.summary: Secure reputation does not require a central authority in every network design. Dynamic Decentralized Reputation System from Blockchain and Secure Multiparty Computation uses blockchain to maintain global reputation and secure multiparty computation to preserve feedback privacy. The reported analysis maintains feedback privacy under a semi-honest model even with n minus 2 dishonest parties, which extends the reputation-infrastructure component of Kaal's claim by identifying a concrete decentralized mechanism. Its reach is narrower than Kaal's proposition. The model does not govern anonymous economic partners or supply dynamic governance. Nor does it establish economy-wide proliferation. This limitation matters because reputation infrastructure is only one of the institutions in the claim.

entry.title: Robust Reputation In Decentralized Markets F88De865
entry.summary: Incomplete information is a separate constraint on reputation-based cooperation. Robust Reputation in Decentralized Markets reports that incomplete information can weaken trust and reputation in open multiagent systems, while gossip-based updates reduced selfishness by up to 25 percent and especially helped agents with little interaction history. This evidence extends Kaal's market-collapse claim because it adds information access as a condition for policeable cooperation, but its scope remains narrow because the study neither establishes collapse in commercial markets nor validates Kaal's broader institutional mechanism. The distinction is important because the source supplies a mitigation mechanism rather than evidence of market failure.

entry.title: Independent Reproduction Interim Estimates
entry.summary:
Breznau and coauthors qualify Kaal's classification of the current estimates as interim. In a computational reproduction experiment, 85 independent teams attempted to reproduce numerical results from the same study. Even the transparent group reproduced 95.7 percent of directions and significance classifications, but only 76.9 percent of estimates within 1 percent of the original values. Only 14 teams reproduced every result within that tolerance. The authors therefore show that access to code improves verification but does not remove researcher error or procedural variation. They estimate that more than one independent attempt may be needed for reliable reproduction.

entry.title: Posttreatment Regrading Treatment Effect
entry.summary:
Post-treatment regrading can compromise a treatment-effect estimate.
Montgomery, Nyhan, and Torres analyze post-treatment conditioning in experiments. They classify three recurring practices: controlling for variables measured after treatment, dropping observations under post-treatment criteria, and restricting samples by post-treatment variables. Their analytical demonstrations and reanalyses show that these choices can distort causal-effect estimates. The direction and size of the bias may not be bounded without strong assumptions. Random assignment does not preserve its identifying advantage once an analysis conditions on information created or selected after treatment.

entry.title: Reputation Mediated Labor Exogenous Demand
entry.summary:
An execution platform can coordinate labor without generating demand.
Kokkodis and Ipeirotis analyze more than one million completed tasks from oDesk. In this market, employers post tasks, remote contractors apply and perform the work, and reputation mechanisms help employers choose among workers whose ability cannot be observed directly before performance. Their models use prior category-specific feedback to predict worker performance. The platform therefore performs two related institutional functions. It coordinates execution and improves matching under uncertainty. The task itself continues to originate with an employer.

entry.title: Tool Capability Economic Persistence Threshold
entry.summary:
Tool capability does not establish autonomous economic persistence.
Qu, Zhao, Zhang, and Song define a self-sovereign agent through distinct operational stages. A tool-capable agent remains sponsor-bound when a human supplies accounts, compute, and payment rails. Economic self-sustainment begins only when the agent controls funds and expected revenue covers inference, tool, cloud, transaction, and retry costs. Persistence requires a further mechanism. The agent must be able to provision new infrastructure and resume operation without human intervention.
This framework qualifies Kaal's negative result. The present system may demonstrate execution inside an externally provisioned environment. entry.title: Externally Provisioned Environment Within Run Selection
entry.summary:
An externally supplied experimental environment does not make the selection process external to the experiment.
Batut, Parsons, Fischer, Beslon, and Knibbe describe in silico experimental evolution. They separate the setup from the operation. Population size, spatial structure, the fitness measure, and selection strength are chosen at the beginning of a run. Within that setup, artificial organisms reproduce and mutate. Fitter organisms reproduce, while other organisms die. This supplies an independent mechanism comparator for Kaal's classification. Selection can operate inside a computational experiment even when the environment and its parameters were provisioned before the run.

entry.title: Descriptive Slope Difference Requires Direct Uncertainty
entry.summary:
The 0.0266 slope difference is an effect estimate. It is not, by itself, a test of whether the selection and random-survival trajectories differ.
Paternoster, Brame, Mazerolle, and Piquero examine direct comparisons between regression slopes. They explain that the difference has its own sampling distribution and standard error. An incorrect standard-error estimator can bias the test toward rejecting equality. This supports Kaal's classification of the 0.0266 value as descriptive. A positive numerical difference may summarize the observed trajectories, but confirmatory inference requires uncertainty for the difference itself.

entry.title: Interval Spanning Zero Does Not Fix Trajectory Direction
entry.summary:
Greenland and coauthors provide an interpretation boundary for the reported interval. Their framework treats an interval as a model-dependent summary of effect sizes that remain more compatible with the data than values outside the range. Kaal reports an aggregate selection slope of 0.0685 and an uncertainty interval from -0.0568 to 0.2020. The range spans negative, null, and positive slopes. It therefore does not fix the direction of the selection trajectory at the interim checkpoint.
The qualification is methodological. Greenland and coauthors analyze confidence intervals and the assumptions that support them. They do not identify Kaal's interval construction, recalculate the slope, inspect the registered estimator, or audit the underlying E2B record. Kaal's source separately classifies the interim estimates as inconclusive. The numerical result remains source-bound.

entry.title: Aiida Qualifies Private Provenance With Selective Disclosure
entry.summary:
Pizzi, Cepellotti, Sabatini, Marzari, and Kozinsky provide an independent implementation precedent for separating evidentiary completeness from public disclosure. AiiDA records calculations and data as nodes joined by directional, labeled links that preserve the causal chain from input data through intermediate calculations to final results. The system stores queryable node attributes and permits users to inspect the history of a computational result. Its sharing design creates a separate boundary. Each user or group may operate a local instance in which data and calculations remain private. A user may then export only a portion of the database to another instance while retaining the remaining private portion.

entry.title: Population Based Training Qualifies Selection Induced Lineage Transition
entry.summary:
Jaderberg, Dalibard, Osindero, Czarnecki, and their coauthors provide an independent operational comparator for a selection-induced lineage transition. The mechanism is concrete. Population Based Training evaluates concurrently trained agents and applies an exploit rule when a population member is ready. Under one reported rule, a lower-performing agent copies the weights and hyperparameters of a better-performing agent, while another rule directs an agent in the bottom fifth to copy from the top fifth. Training then continues from the inherited model state. The authors represent each executed exploit operation as a branch in the full phylogenetic tree because the parameters were copied. The transition is therefore an implemented change in model ancestry rather than a descriptive label.

entry.title: Darwin Godel Machine Qualifies Generation Boundary Continuity
entry.summary:
Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, and Clune provide an independent comparator for the claimed generation boundary. Their Darwin Gödel Machine begins with one coding agent and preserves discovered agents in an archive. At each iteration, the system selects a parent, uses the parent to produce a modified child, evaluates the child, and admits only agents that retain the capacity for further self-modification. The authors report that this cycle continued for 80 iterations. The archive permits an earlier result to seed later work even when the relevant lineage is not selected in every intervening iteration. This evidence establishes that an agentic computation can preserve lineage and continue activity across completed evolutionary cycles.

entry.title: Stateful Evolution Supports Feasibility Not Drift Identification
entry.summary:
State must persist before an evolutionary trajectory can be evaluated. Lalan, Ghosh, Kolsur, and Dutta implement a stateful multi-agent search for unit-test generation. A controller carries edge cases, coverage scores, mutation feedback, exception signals, and reward history across successive stages. Later stages inherit and refine earlier judgments. A critic scores candidates, while evolutionary selection preserves a population of high-performing elites. The reported system achieves higher coverage than stateless prompting baselines.
This evidence qualifies Kaal's E2B question. It shows that an artificial agent process can preserve evaluation-relevant state across evolutionary stages and condition later candidates on that history. The resulting search is selected and history dependent rather than a sequence of isolated samples.

entry.summary:

Their framework separates the treatment label from the version that determines the potential outcome. It permits version-specific comparisons and policy-level averages over assigned versions. Those quantities are not interchangeable. An overall average remains tied to the distribution and assignment policy for treatment versions.
This analysis qualifies Kaal's treatment of a broader comparison. A comparison that changes the agent, task, or model binding can be interpreted as changing the version of the experimental condition. entry.title: Matched Protocols Narrow Agent Workflow Attribution
entry.summary:
Matched comparisons require more than common outcome labels. Fu and colleagues ask whether reorganizing a single-agent workflow into a multi-agent workflow changes accuracy and cost. Their BenchAgent design holds the base model, benchmark loader, tool interface, answer contract, evaluator, and accounting substrate constant. It also records agent identifiers and stage-level traces under one execution system. The measured difference can therefore be assigned more narrowly to workflow organization.
This evidence qualifies Kaal's strict matched-analysis requirement. The source binds the compared workflows to the same base model and benchmark inputs. It also keeps the execution and evaluation surfaces common and preserves the identifiers needed to reconstruct agent activity. entry.title: Reputation Links Current Conduct To Future Work
entry.summary:
Reputation links current conduct to future work. Benson, Sojourner, and Umyarov study Amazon Mechanical Turk, where employers may keep completed work without paying and workers cannot rely on ordinary contract enforcement. Their model treats an employer's payment history as a public relational contract. The threat of losing future workers discourages opportunism. Their field experiments then show that employers with good reputations attract workers more quickly and at a larger scale without reducing work quality. Workers for good-reputation employers also earn 40 percent higher effective wages because tasks finish faster and rejection is less likely.

entry.title: Classification Does Not Establish Institutional Displacement
entry.summary:
Classification does not establish displacement. Reimers, Guo, and Li classify three institutionally distinct two-sided markets as functional alternatives to markets, hybrids, and hierarchies. They then separate that classification from a prediction about organizational change. A technology that enables a new form does not establish that the new form will replace an existing one. The inference requires conditions and trade-offs that can decide the outcome in a concrete situation.
This distinction independently extends Kaal's inference boundary. Classifying two institutional arrangements identifies their differences. It does not show that one arrangement universally displaces the other. A displacement proposition requires additional evidence about the conditions under which the relevant trade-offs favor a shift.

entry.title: Centralized And Decentralized Reputation Allocate Evaluation Differently
entry.summary:
Evaluative authority has an institutional location. Noorian and Ulieru classify centralized reputation systems by a central database and authority that receive transaction reports, aggregate ratings, and calculate public scores. Their decentralized category removes that location. Each agent stores ratings and uses a tailored computation engine to calculate and validate the trustworthiness of a potential partner.
This classification independently extends Kaal's distinction. A centralized reward model and cohort-governed reputation do not merely apply different techniques to the same evaluator. They allocate the collection, computation, and validation of evaluative information to different actors.
The correspondence is limited. Noorian and Ulieru study trust and reputation systems in online communities and open multi-agent systems. They do not analyze reward modeling, Kaal's cohort desig

entry.title: Verification Technology Can Expand The Firm Boundary
entry.summary:
Baker and Hubbard make firm boundaries observable as a response to verification technology. Using detailed trucking data, they examine whether on-board computers changed the contractibility of driver actions and, through that change, truck ownership. Adoption reduced driver ownership, especially for long hauls. It moved production toward more integrated asset ownership. The result supports Kaal's proposition that a firm's boundary can vary with the technology used to verify performance. It also qualifies it sharply: better verification did not make the firm disappear. In this setting, it reduced independent contracting and produced larger firms.
The comparison remains bounded. On-board computers monitored truck drivers in one industry. They did not test autonomous agents, computational abundance, or Kaal's residual verification architecture, and the results do not establish that every i

entry.title: Delegated Monitoring Costs Depend On Scale And Diversification
entry.summary:
Douglas Diamond studies a financial intermediary. His model treats monitoring information as an input that resolves incentive problems between borrowers and lenders. Delegation creates an additional cost because lenders must motivate the intermediary to monitor. Diversification within the intermediary reduces that cost, even under risk neutrality. Scale matters. Monitoring can therefore become economically viable when institutional scale changes the cost of producing credible oversight, which qualifies Kaal's classification of monitoring as a production-economics question.
The correspondence is bounded. Diamond studies lenders, borrowers, and financial intermediaries rather than autonomous agents. He does not analyze Kaal's validation architecture or any specific funding mechanism. The model does not show that monitoring supports itself at every scale. It identifies conditions under whi

entry.title: Permissionless Trust Support Requires Recurring Compensation
entry.summary: Budish gives economic content to Kaal's distinction between internal stake accounting and external resource finance. His zero-profit condition treats trust support as costly work, stake, storage, or memory and makes the quantity supplied a function of protocol compensation. The resulting equilibrium constraint requires recurring payment for trust support to be large relative to the benefits of attack. This supports Kaal's condition that internal accounting alone does not finance external verification resources. It does not establish that Kaal's reference mechanism lacks an external financing channel, measure its infrastructure costs, or extend beyond permissionless consensus.

entry.title: Anonymous Random Matching Folk Theorem Conditions
entry.summary: Deb, Sugaya, and Wolitzky sharply bound Kaal's use of the anonymous-random-matching Folk Theorem. They prove a Folk Theorem for discounted repeated games with anonymous random matching, allowing nonuniform matching and asymmetric payoffs, but retain full dimensionality as a stage-game condition. Their result supports treating the theorem as a conditional benchmark within that model. It does not provide a general performance floor for an implemented reputation mechanism, predict which equilibrium will occur, or establish any outcome in Kaal's reference system.

entry.title: Causal Mediation Mechanism Attribution
entry.summary: Imai, Keele, Tingley, and Yamamoto sharpen Kaal's attribution rule. They define a causal mechanism through a mediator and show that identifying the mechanism requires explicit assumptions, mediation analysis, sensitivity analysis, or research designs that manipulate the mediator. A randomized treatment can identify an overall effect without identifying how that effect arose. The source therefore supports Kaal's demand for mechanism-specific evidence. It also narrows it. Randomizing treatment and the intermediate variable is not automatically sufficient, and ablation is not examined. Attribution remains conditional on the mediator, estimand, design, and identification assumptions.

entry.title: Causal Equivalence Bounds Observational Attribution
entry.summary: Squires and Uhler qualify Kaal's attribution boundary. They show that observational data can identify an equivalence class of causal graphs rather than a unique graph. Graphs within the class encode the same conditional independence relations even when their edge directions differ. Interventional data can refine the class. The result supports the narrower proposition that a downstream observable does not, by itself, identify the architecture that generated it. The limitation is equally important. The source concerns causal directed acyclic graphs under formal assumptions, not Kaal's institutional architecture or its registered metrics. It does not establish non-identifiability when stronger distributional assumptions, experiments, or domain restrictions identify a unique structure.

entry.title: Majority Aggregation Preserves Measurable Judgment Uncertainty
entry.summary: Davani, Díaz, and Prabhakaran qualify Kaal's treatment of cohort judgment as an estimator rather than a truth oracle. Across seven binary classification tasks, they show that majority voting can erase systematic annotator disagreement. Their multi-annotator model matches or improves predictive performance and produces uncertainty estimates that better track disagreement. This supports the narrower proposition that aggregation leaves measurable uncertainty and that a naive aggregate can conceal structure in the judgments it combines. The limitation is material. Their tasks concern subjective language annotation, not Kaal's verification cohort. The source does not validate Kaal's variance calculation, reproduce Part VI.C, or show that every form of verification preserves information asymmetry.

entry.title: Crowd Aggregation Error Is Bounded Only Under Explicit Conditions
entry.summary: Li and Yu qualify Kaal's shift from persistent asymmetry to a measurable residual. Under the Dawid-Skene crowdsourcing model, they derive finite-sample exponential bounds for aggregation error and identify task assignment, worker reliability, and normalized score gaps as conditions on those bounds. Their result supports the narrower proposition that aggregate judgment error can be measured and controlled by design. The limitation is decisive. The bound is conditional on a specified labeling model and aggregation rule. It does not show that information asymmetry generally contracts, test Kaal's reputation-weighted pool, or establish that residual error will shrink under unmodeled dependence or strategic behavior.

entry.title: Computational Ai Output Makes Institutional Verification Scarce
entry.summary: Dogonowski identifies a corresponding institutional constraint in AI deployment. Computational capability scales faster than an organization's capacity to validate AI-mediated outputs. The model therefore treats verification, not generation, as the binding constraint on safe deployment and shows how costly verification can produce a stable zero-verification equilibrium. This independently extends Kaal's proposition that abundant individual computation can relocate boundedness to institutional verification capacity. The evidence is limited to a posted organizational model. It does not establish that computation exceeds every decision requirement, or that aggregation and collective action are the only remaining constraints.

entry.title: Abundant Idea Generation Moves The Bottleneck To Evaluation
entry.summary: Qiao and colleagues identify a corresponding displacement in automated science. Large language models now produce research ideas at unprecedented scale, while evaluation still depends on scarce expert judgment. This independently extends Kaal's proposition that computationally cheap ideation moves the binding constraint toward determining which candidates are sound, feasible, and significant. The evidence is limited to scientific research ideas. It does not establish that ideation has zero marginal cost, that evaluation is the only remaining constraint, or that InnoEval resolves safety and alignment.

entry.title: Reputation Prediction Must Separate Representation From Information
entry.summary:
Kokkodis and Ipeirotis show that reputation design affects prediction. Their model replaces an undifferentiated average of prior feedback with category-specific histories and cross-category weights. On held-out oDesk transactions, this representation reduces prediction error relative to aggregate-history baselines. The result supports testing whether a structured reputation signal contains information for future task performance that a simpler outcome-history summary omits.
The comparison also narrows Kaal's H2. The external model constructs reputation from prior employer ratings. It does not compare an independently generated reputation measure with the full observed outcome history. It therefore does not establish that reputation adds information beyond outcomes as such. The source studies human online labor markets, not multi-model agents or Kaal's registered Stage 4 design. Its cont

entry.title: Matching Defines The Target Estimand
entry.summary: Greifer and Stuart clarify what a matched comparison can establish. Matching does not supply a generic treatment effect. It defines an effect for a target population, and different matching procedures can change that population. The authors therefore require the estimand and statistical method to be aligned before interpreting an outcome difference. This qualification supports Kaal's formulation of H1 as a question about output quality under a properly matched estimand. It does not establish that the joint substrate improves output quality. The source studies observational treatment comparisons, not multi-model agents or Kaal's registered Stage 4 design. Its contribution is methodological. A difference in outcomes is interpretable only for the population and causal assumptions encoded by the chosen estimand.

entry.title: Null Evidence Does Not Uniquely Identify A Mechanism
entry.summary:
Fanelli extends Kaal's identification limit for null evidence. A null or negative result can rule out a tested hypothesis under the stated design. It does not thereby select a unique explanation. Fanelli models the knowledge value of a negative result as declining with the number of hypotheses, methods, explanations, or outcomes that remain untested. Real experiments retain uncertainty because several alternative hypotheses can remain compatible with the same outcome. The problem persists even with greater statistical power when auxiliary assumptions remain uncontrolled.
The correspondence is narrow. Fanelli supplies a general meta-scientific account of negative-result informativeness. The article does not test Kaal's computational economy, reconstruct his empirical condition, or identify the mechanism behind any particular null. It supports the distinction between disciplining a condit

entry.title: Code Verification Does Not Establish Economic Effects
entry.summary:
Code establishes a model's implementation. Economic effects require separate evidence. Gräbner's validation framework explains the distinction. Model verification tests whether a computational model does what its designer intended. Validation asks whether the model reasonably represents its target and assesses the model's relationship to reality. His framework also requires an explicit key between model properties and target-system properties. Validation becomes necessary when the model is used to make informed statements about the real world.
This independently qualifies Kaal's claim. Formal objects and source code can make a mechanism explicit and testable. They do not show that the named economic effect occurred. That inference requires observable target properties and an appropriate validation design.
The source concerns computational models generally. The analysis does not evaluat

entry.title: Agent Benchmarks Do Not Establish Production Transfer
entry.summary: Kapoor and coauthors qualify Kaal's external-validity limit. They show that agent benchmark accuracy may not translate to real-world performance when benchmarks permit shortcuts or omit appropriate holdouts. They also identify distribution shifts that benchmark designers cannot fully model and recommend comparing benchmark results with corresponding real-world tasks. This supports Kaal's decision to confine the Article's findings to its disclosed research setting. It does not establish how the Agentic Reputation Substrate performs at production scale. The source does not test Kaal's cohort, reputation treatment, deliberation protocol, agency-cost measures, or deployment environment. Production effects may therefore persist, amplify, or invert. The present evidence does not decide among those outcomes.

entry.title: Debate Composition Does Not Upgrade Agent Intelligence
entry.summary: Zhu and coauthors qualify Kaal's interpretation of deliberation as a composition intervention. In their controlled model, homogeneous agents with unweighted updates preserve expected correctness during debate. Diversity-aware initialization improves the prior probability that a correct hypothesis is present, but does not change the subsequent update dynamics. Confidence-weighted debate changes how answers are aggregated. The result supports a distinction between the composition and protocol of a debating group and the underlying intelligence of any one model. It does not establish Kaal's empirical conclusion. The source uses reasoning benchmarks and a Dirichlet-categorical model. It does not test monitoring, Kaal's controlled cohort, the Agentic Reputation Substrate, campaign units, or the observed composition of error. Kaal's claim remains limited to the completed treatment under the re

entry.title: Explore Confirm Separation Does Not Prove A Null Effect
entry.summary: Thibault and coauthors provide a methodological qualification to the registered null result. Their Explore and Confirm Analysis Workflow permits exploration on a data subset, but requires the resulting analysis script to be registered before access to the full dataset. The design preserves a confirmatory test on data not used to develop the analysis. That mechanism corresponds to Kaal's separation of the discovery run from confirmation. It does not establish that net discrimination was absent. It also does not recalculate the reported estimate or interval, examine Kaal's campaign units, or audit adherence to the preregistration. The external source supports the discovery-to-confirmation design logic only. Kaal's numerical result remains source-bound to the Article.

entry.title: Pooled Confidence Does Not Establish Cross Setting Prediction
entry.summary: IntHout, Ioannidis, Rovers, and Goeman qualify the inference from a pooled confidence interval. Under between-study heterogeneity, a pooled 95 percent confidence interval may remain wholly on one side of zero while a prediction interval reaches both sides. Their review found that 72.4 percent of statistically significant Cochrane meta-analyses with observed heterogeneity had prediction intervals that included the null. This result does not dispute the registered calculation or the negative direction in each campaign unit. It shows that pooled significance and directional consistency do not alone establish how the effect will generalize to another exchangeable unit. That stronger claim requires a heterogeneity-aware prediction analysis. The paper does not test Kaal's cohort, hypotheses, estimator, or campaign units.

entry.title: Null Result Does Not Establish Zero Effect
entry.summary: The inference remains bounded. Pawel and coauthors show that a non-significant estimate does not by itself establish the absence of an effect. The reported interval crosses zero and remains compatible with effects from -0.0502 to +0.0985. The result therefore leaves direction unresolved under the reported design. It does not show that the effect equals zero. Evidence for absence requires a method designed for that question, such as equivalence testing or a Bayes factor. This qualification does not recalculate Kaal's estimate, identify an equivalence margin, or test the registered endpoint, the multi-model cohort, or the Agentic Reputation Substrate. It limits the interpretation to what the estimate and confidence interval can support.

entry.title: Assignment Control Removes One Causal Bias Channel
entry.summary: Hennessy and Strebulaev sharpen the inference boundary. Their model treats government policy as an independent stochastic process, which allows them to abstract from endogeneity bias. Yet they show that random assignment alone does not make measured treatment responses equal causal effects in dynamic economies. Additional identifying assumptions remain necessary. This qualification supports holding work assignment fixed when the objective is to separate an institution's effect on outcomes from its effect on work selection. It does not establish that the matched condition identifies every causal effect. The paper studies dynamic policy environments, not multi-model agents, validation pools, or Kaal's registered cohort. Its contribution is narrower: controlling assignment can remove one selection channel without resolving every source of causal bias.

entry.title: Production Systems Require Evidence Beyond Academic Design
entry.summary: Paleyes, Urma, and Lawrence distinguish academic machine learning from deployment in a real-world production system. Their survey identifies challenges at every stage of the deployment workflow. This supports treating a proposed production system as a separate evidentiary object. It does not validate Kaal's registered forward program, the Agentic Reputation Substrate, or any production implementation.

entry.title: Scientific Evidence Is Bound To The Tested Research Apparatus
entry.summary:
Scientific evidence is apparatus-bound. Kanewala and Bieman's systematic review explains why. The review reports that scientific software generates evidence for research publications, while also finding that testing is often limited to the initial scientific problem addressed by the code. Reliability on a different problem therefore cannot be guaranteed. This supports treating the completed E1 and E2a evidence as evidence about the historical research apparatus that produced it.
The relationship is a qualification. The review does not examine Kaal's apparatus, autonomous agents, either experiment, or the current reference implementation, and it cannot establish which code, models, or institutional conditions produced Kaal's results. Those facts remain source-bound to Kaal's Article. The external evidence instead supplies the methodological reason for keeping the completed evidence tied

entry.title: Deliberation Does Not Guarantee Net Group Intelligence
entry.summary: Lu, Yuan, and McLeod qualify Kaal's narrow account of the promoted deliberation hypotheses. Their meta-analysis covers 65 hidden-profile studies, 101 independent effects, and 3,189 groups. Hidden-profile groups discussed substantially more common than unique information and were eight times less likely to find the solution than full-information groups. Information coverage and discussion focus were positively related to decision quality, but group size, information load, task demonstrability, and hidden-profile strength moderated the results. The evidence supports a limited inference: deliberation can change which information reaches the group without making the pool smarter in net. The study concerns human groups and hidden-profile tasks. It does not test autonomous agents, Kaal's cohort, or either registered hypothesis.

entry.title: Information Diversity Reduces Prevote Unanimity
entry.summary: Markou and Chan extend Kaal's prediction that deliberation should reduce unanimity. They analyze verbatim transcripts from Food and Drug Administration advisory committee meetings before and after a change from sequential to simultaneous voting. Unanimous votes became less likely. The increased diversity of information surfaced during prevote discussions mediated most of that reduction. Members also asked one another more questions and shared speaking time more equally. This evidence supports the narrower mechanism that discussion can expose individually held information before votes bind. The institutional change altered voting rules and discussion incentives together. It does not isolate deliberation as the sole treatment, identify articulated disagreement as the only channel, test autonomous agents, or measure Kaal's cascade construct. The registered prediction therefore remains unver

entry.title: Reflective Exchange Exposes Unknowns Before Approval
entry.summary: Piehlmaier qualifies Kaal's prediction that deliberation should reduce over-approval. His preregistered experiments distinguish reflective exchange from validation. Joint financial decision-making reduced overconfidence when the interaction made unknown aspects of the decision salient. A simple stamp of approval without reflection did not provide the same corrective mechanism. This supports a narrower causal rationale. An exchange can expose missing information before a decision hardens. The study does not examine agentic validator pools, submission approval, reputation-bearing incentives, profit from approval, or Kaal's registered cohort. It measures investor overconfidence in controlled financial-decision settings. The predicted effect on false approvals therefore remains unverified until the registered study tests it directly.

entry.title: Fixed Conditions Isolate Treatment Effect
entry.summary: Hunt, Stringer, and Polagye qualify Kaal's fixed-conditions design. Their turbine experiment held confinement, Froude number, Reynolds number, and other non-dimensional parameters constant while varying aspect ratio. When they relaxed the Froude-number control, the resulting efficiency increase could have been misattributed to aspect ratio. This supports the causal rationale for fixing treatment-relevant conditions. The correspondence remains methodological. The source studies a hydraulic turbine, not agentic validators or a multi-model cohort. It does not verify that Kaal held every relevant condition fixed. It also shows that identifying every relevant control is difficult and that an omitted condition can change the inference.

entry.title: Structured Assessment Precedes Final Verdict
entry.summary: Structured assessment changes a decision process only if the assessment arrives before judgment. That sequence matters. Harrasse, Bandi, and Bandi route paired LLM evaluations through advocates, a criteria-based judge, and an independent jury that renders the final verdict. D3 compares that deliberative architecture with a single judge that selects directly. On MT-Bench, D3-MORE reports 85.1 percent accuracy, 12.6 percentage points above the single-judge baseline. This result qualifies Kaal's treatment-control design. It supports separating an assessment-exchange treatment from a no-exchange adjudication baseline. Yet the study does not establish a matched control with identical token budgets or Kaal's validator incentives, binding rules, and reputation consequences. The correspondence is limited to the comparative design and its measured evaluation setting. Deliberation has evidentiary

entry.title: Majority Pressure Suppresses Independent Correction
entry.summary: Majority pressure is an information channel, not a substitute for independent judgment. Wu, Li, and Li begin their controlled LLM debate with independent proposals. They then find that agents facing an incorrect majority are less able to correct the group, particularly when the agents are weaker. This result qualifies Kaal's information-isolating validation claim. It independently supports preserving an initial judgment before a participant sees a running tally or peer argument. It does not test Kaal's staged procedure, reputation-bearing consequences, or cohort-mediated accountability. The correspondence is therefore limited to the cascade mechanism. Independence must be preserved before deliberation can improve collective judgment.

entry.title: Peer Rated Task Performance Changes Agent Reputation
entry.summary: Lou et al. provide a narrow operational analogue to Kaal's standing mechanism. Their DRF framework raises an LLM agent's reputation when its peer-derived task score meets the task threshold and lowers reputation when the score falls below it. The source supports performance-contingent gains and losses in standing. It does not establish independent or cryptographic verification, and it tests a simulated rating network rather than Kaal's substrate.

entry.title: Nontransferable Reputation Coordinates Agent Systems
entry.summary:
Architecture comes first. Touloupou and Kapassa supply an independent specification for Kaal's definitional claim. Their systematic survey treats agent registries as a first coordination layer through which agents announce capabilities and discover counterparties without a centralized directory. Separately, the authors classify reputation accumulated from past behavior as a longer-horizon coordination substrate because non-transferability prevents purchase and ties standing to actual agent history rather than financial position.
This extends Kaal's substrate definition. Persistent reputation is not merely descriptive metadata. In the surveyed architecture, it informs counterparty discovery, task-market verification, and decentralized quality filtering. Yet the source separates identity, registries, task markets, settlement, and reputation. That distinction matters. It supports a coordin

entry.title: Timestamp Evidence Does Not Prove Later Events
entry.summary:
Public timestamps establish a narrow temporal proposition. Birkholz, Fossati, and Riechert distinguish timestamps covering payload data from timestamps covering a cryptographic signature. A payload timestamp proves that the payload existed at an earlier point. It does not establish when a separate signature was created. The authors warn that treating it as such can cause validators to accept signatures produced after key revocation.
This distinction qualifies Kaal's claim directly. His public timestamp establishes that the attested artifact existed no later than the recorded time. Further conclusions require evidence bound to each later event. The timestamp alone does not prove execution, deployment, review, or any subsequent operational step.
The source concerns COSE messages and RFC 3161 tokens. It does not audit Kaal's artifact or provenance chain. It also does not determine whether

entry.title: Confirmatory Analysis Requires Prospective Constraint
entry.summary:
Confirmatory analysis depends on when analytical discretion closes. Watt and Kennedy require every analysis decision capable of affecting confirmatory results to be made before data collection. They include statistical methods, evidence criteria, data transformations, and exclusion rules. This provides an external benchmark for Kaal's design. Kaal fixed directional hypotheses, a bootstrap estimator, exclusions, a randomization audit, a data-quality gate, and the confirmation rule before confirmatory computation.
The benchmark also narrows the claim. Watt and Kennedy use a stronger timing rule than Kaal's statement. Their standard closes analytical discretion before data collection, while Kaal's source-bound claim establishes closure before confirmatory computation. The article does not audit Kaal's preregistration, determine when his data became available, reproduce the bootstrap, or va

entry.title: Deliberative Quality Is Not Disagreement For Its Own Sake
entry.summary:
Niemeyer, Veri, Dryzek, and Bächtiger qualify Kaal's prediction about deliberation and unanimity. Their account does not treat opinion change, disagreement, or raw agreement as sufficient evidence of deliberative quality. Opinion change may arise from polarization, while high agreement may still fail to express deliberative reason. The authors instead ask whether a group has integrated relevant considerations within a shared representational framework. Agreement and disagreement matter only when judgments remain coherent with that framework.
The distinction gives Kaal's prediction a limited institutional meaning. A reduction in unanimity may be relevant when deliberation exposes considerations that earlier votes failed to integrate, but the resulting divergence is not itself the objective. It indicates a representational update only when participants respond to relevant reasons and thei

entry.title: Uniform Actions Do Not Uniquely Identify Information Cascades
entry.summary:
Çelen and Kariv extend Kaal's caution that unanimous verdicts do not, by themselves, identify an information cascade. Their experiment separates observed actions from underlying beliefs. A herd begins when participants take the same action. A cascade requires the stronger condition that they act without regard to private signals. The authors elicit signal cutoffs before each participant sees the private signal. This allows them to distinguish conformity in realized actions from decisions that no possible private signal would change. They find frequent herding and cascades, but not every observed herd is a cascade. The result supports Kaal's treatment of unanimity as a cascade-consistent quantity rather than a unique diagnostic.
Scope matters. The experiment uses sequential human decisions with continuous private signals and binary actions. It does not study validators, LLM agents, work-

entry.title: Rating Inflation Qualifies Monitoring Layer Moral Hazard
entry.summary:
Bolton, Freixas, and Shapiro qualify Kaal's treatment of over-approval as moral hazard in the monitoring layer. Their model places the conflict inside the rating agency. The agency can understate credit risk to attract business, while issuers can purchase only favorable ratings. Rating inflation becomes more likely when reputation costs are lower or more investors accept ratings at face value. The monitor's verdict can therefore become more favorable even when the underlying risk remains unchanged. This correspondence supports Kaal's classification of over-approval as an incentive failure by the adjudicator rather than merely an error by the worker being evaluated.
The comparison is bounded. Credit rating agencies evaluate securities, not LLM-generated task outputs. The source models reported credit risk rather than approval against a known task-level ground truth. It does not test Kaal

entry.title: Construct Validity Qualifies External Metric Anchoring
entry.summary: Cronbach and Meehl qualify Kaal's external-anchoring rule. Their account of construct validity requires a nomological network that connects a test, its construct, other constructs, and observable quantities. The network must make contact with observations through public steps of inference. It must also be stated clearly enough for other researchers to accept or reject it. A failed prediction cannot be cured by redefining the construct after the result. A changed interpretation requires fresh data. This supports Kaal's insistence that the agency-cost battery rest on definitions and relations external to the Article's own conclusions. Otherwise, the battery risks becoming insulated from disconfirming evidence. The correspondence is methodological, not empirical. Cronbach and Meehl do not study LLM agents, reputation systems, or Kaal's nine metrics. Their analysis does not show that any sel

entry.title: Reputation Treatment Qualifies Institutional Layer Experiment
entry.summary: Knutsen and Heggedal qualify Kaal's experimental design. Their laboratory study compares three repeated-game conditions. The control reveals no history. A second treatment exposes past actions. A third treatment adds induced commitment types and permits reputation formation. Efficient coordination in late supergames rises from 5 percent in the control to 50 percent with history and 84 percent with the reputation treatment. The design supports isolating a reputation mechanism by varying the institutional layer around a fixed underlying game. Its scope is narrower than Kaal's program. The subjects are human players in repeated coordination games. The source does not use heterogeneous AI agents, conventional ground-truthed tasks, or a combined reputation-and-incentive layer. It also does not compare that combined layer with its absence. The external experiment therefore supports the treatme

entry.title: Small Group Deliberation Qualifies Controlled Collective Accuracy
entry.summary: Navajas et al. qualify Kaal's empirical deliberation claim. The comparison is narrow. In a live crowd of 5,180 participants, individuals first answered general knowledge questions, then deliberated in independent groups of five, reached consensus, and revised their estimates. Averaging the group decisions was more accurate than aggregating the initial independent answers. The experiment thus shows that group structure can change the measured effect of deliberation under controlled conditions, but it does not test a reputation-bearing validation institution. It also does not involve autonomous agents, preregistration, replication, or Kaal's metric definitions and correction procedure. The human participants answered general knowledge questions, not tasks assigned to a controlled multi-model cohort. Kaal's reported result therefore remains source-bound to the registered cohort and cannot b

entry.title: Registered Reports Qualify Discovery Confirmation Cycle
entry.summary: Arpinon and Lefebvre qualify Kaal's discovery-to-confirmation design. Registered Reports fix the analysis plan before data collection. In-principle acceptance then commits the journal to publication regardless of the result, subject to Stage 2 verification that the analysis followed the Stage 1 plan. Their format also separates confirmatory analyses from later exploration and prevents conclusions from resting on ex-post exploratory results. This correspondence is limited. The article addresses a journal review format in agricultural economics. It does not verify Kaal's registered primary, the reporting of his null result, the preregistration of any exploratory signal, or the mechanical application of his confirmation rule. It also warns that preregistration alone leaves room for incomplete plans, uncertain policing, and suppression of null findings. Kaal's cycle therefore tracks recogniz

entry.title: Preregistration Methods Qualify Registered Design Control
entry.summary: Rubin qualifies Kaal's registered design claim. Preregistration places planned hypotheses, methods, and analyses in a time-stamped record before data collection and analysis. That historical record allows readers to identify deviations between the plan and the reported study. The correspondence is limited. The source does not verify that Kaal's hypotheses, metric definitions, correction procedure, or analysis plan were fixed before each condition ran. It also argues that preregistration supplies historical transparency, not a complete credibility judgment, when current rationales, open materials, code, and robustness checks are available. Kaal's claim therefore describes a relevant design control. Its execution and evidentiary weight still depend on the preserved registration, disclosed deviations, and the study record.

entry.title: Multiagentbench Qualifies Nine Metric Agent Comparison
entry.summary: Zhu and colleagues qualify Kaal's nine-metric comparison. MultiAgentBench evaluates multi-agent systems across two dimensions: task completion and coordination. It combines milestone-based KPIs and final-output scores with planning and communication measures. This supports a multidimensional battery when the object of study includes both outcomes and interaction processes. The correspondence is limited. MultiAgentBench uses six scenarios and its own scoring instruments. It does not validate Kaal's nine labels, the reliability or calibration of those measures, the registered cohort, or any resulting comparison. The source also reports limited scenario and model coverage. Finer-grained component analysis remains future work.

entry.title: Experimental Economics Qualifies Fixed Cohort Institutional Comparison
entry.summary: Bougherara, Muller, and Teyssier qualify Kaal's controlled comparison. They explain that experimental economics isolates a causal effect by changing one environmental or institutional feature at a time. Within-subject designs can hold the participants constant across treatments, but they also create an order-effect risk. This supports the methodological rationale for keeping the labor force and work assignment fixed while varying the institution. The correspondence remains narrow. The chapter states a general experimental principle. It does not verify that Kaal's cohort, tasks, or timing were actually held constant. It also does not establish randomization, counterbalancing, independence across conditions, or the validity of any later estimate.

entry.title: Wolf Qualifies Deliberation Error Composition Through Quorum Responses
entry.summary: Wolf and colleagues qualify Kaal's exploratory result. In a human predator-detection experiment, participants first decided alone and then observed the choices of other group members. Mean true positives rose from 0.564 to 0.751. Mean false positives fell from 0.166 to 0.113. The source therefore provides independent evidence that group interaction can change the composition of decision errors. The correspondence remains narrow. Wolf and colleagues studied a quorum response under conditionally independent personal information. Their intervention improved both sides of discrimination. It did not leave net discrimination unchanged. The study also did not examine autonomous agents, over-approval, unanimity, or herding. It does not validate Kaal's design, execution, or reported effect sizes.

entry.title: Etherington Qualifies Reduced Action Intensity Through Peer Discussion
entry.summary: Etherington and colleagues qualify Kaal's exploratory result. In a multicenter vignette study, internal medicine residents first decided alone and then deliberated in small peer groups. Discussion reduced practice intensity and increased clinical certainty beyond the result expected from averaging individual scores. Practice intensity meant willingness to order tests, consultations, or treatment. That result offers narrow evidence that discussion can lower action intensity through interaction. Still, the correspondence does not establish better decisions. The instrument did not measure whether less intense practice was appropriate, and the study did not examine autonomous agents or work-product approval. It also provides no evidence on unanimity, net discrimination, or Kaal's reported effects.

entry.title: Henderson Chambers Qualify Exploratory Effects As Tentative Hypotheses
entry.summary: Henderson and Chambers qualify Kaal's treatment of exploratory effects with Registered Report guidance. They state that data-dependent exploratory analyses generate hypotheses rather than test them. Such results should remain tentative until further confirmatory research verifies them. This supports Kaal's decision to label the two discovery-campaign effects as hypotheses rather than findings. The correspondence is methodological. The source does not evaluate Kaal's agents, experimental execution, effect sizes, or whether later work confirmed either effect.

entry.title: Klein Epley Qualify Reduced Over Approval Through Group Lie Detection
entry.summary: Klein and Epley qualify Kaal's exploratory over-approval result with four experiments on human lie detection. Three-person groups that discussed their judgments distinguished truths from lies more accurately than individuals. The gain came primarily from identifying lies correctly, not from improved truth detection or a change in the tendency to answer 'lie.' Statistical aggregation of individual answers did not reproduce the effect. The source therefore supports a narrow mechanism correspondence: discussion can reduce acceptance of false content through information created in interaction. The comparison remains limited. The experiments concern human judgments about deceptive statements. They do not test multi-model validation pools, ground-truth work approval, unanimity, or Kaal's reported effect sizes.

entry.title: Lorenz Qualifies Deliberation Null Through Convergence Without Accuracy Gain
entry.summary: Lorenz and colleagues qualify Kaal's registered null result with an independent experiment on collective judgment. Social influence caused participants' estimates to converge and reduced group diversity. It did not significantly reduce collective error or improve accuracy. The result establishes that information exchange can change group behavior without improving the relevant accuracy measure. The correspondence is limited. Lorenz and colleagues study human factual estimation under exposure to others' answers. They do not study structured multi-model validation pools, Youden's J, or Kaal's reported confidence interval.

entry.title: Dirnagl Qualifies Two Act Cycle Through Exploration And Confirmation
entry.summary: Dirnagl qualifies Kaal's two-act empirical cycle with an independent methodological rationale for separating discovery from confirmation. Exploratory work develops theories, hypotheses, methods, and evidence to carry forward. The same data cannot both generate and test a hypothesis, so a distinct confirmatory phase must follow to screen false positives and inflated effects. Dirnagl also argues that preregistration and contemporaneous logging should preserve the study's trajectory, including methodological choices and failed lines of experimentation. That makes the process itself evidentiary, not merely the final numbers. The correspondence is methodological only. Dirnagl writes from biomedical research and does not evaluate Kaal's multi-agent cohort, registered measures, execution, or reported effects.

The witness-reputation component also improved and accelerated agent learning within the consumer community. It separately rewards experts for faithfully reporting probability estimates and converts the scores into training rewards or evaluation payoffs. Under stated prior assumptions, honest and informative reporting is a payoff-maximizing equilibrium. Experiments across models from 135M to 405B parameters and 85 domains show resistance to deceptive answers and recovery of most of the truthfulness loss after malicious fine-tuning. entry.title: Cattle Trade Tests Llm Agents Under Conflicting Incentives
entry.summary: Müller and Müller extend Kaal's diagnosis by testing LLM agents in an explicitly incentive-bearing environment. Cattle Trade places four agents in a 50–60-turn economic game combining auctions, hidden offers, bargaining, bluffing, opponent modeling, resource constraints, and conflicting incentives. Across 242 games, the authors find that strategic coherence is more closely associated with success than any isolated capability. Their behavior traces also expose overbidding, self-bidding, bankrupt trade initiation, and weak opponent-state adaptation. This does not validate Kaal's reputation substrate. It is a bounded benchmark that moves multi-agent evaluation beyond capability-only tests toward behavior under economic and adversarial incentives.

entry.title: Folk Theorem Equilibrium Existence Does Not Select Cooperation
entry.summary: Jindani independently confirms Kaal's distinction between equilibrium existence and equilibrium selection. His peer-reviewed analysis states that the Folk Theorem permits a wide range of payoffs in infinitely repeated games, while existing learning results that converge to equilibrium do not select among those equilibria. Jindani then adds a stochastic learning rule that selects an efficient subgame-perfect equilibrium. The extension is narrow. The result concerns two-player repeated games under specified learning dynamics. It does not show that an autonomous-agent population will select cooperation merely because cooperative equilibria are available.

entry.title: Signed Content Hashes Enable Independent Evidence Verification
entry.summary: Elliott, Poelen, and Fortes independently support the content-addressed verification mechanism in Kaal's evidentiary-base claim. Their peer-reviewed Scientific Data article shows that signed citations bind digital content to unique, recomputable content signatures. A future reader can verify content identity by recomputing the hash, and recursively signed references can form verifiable citation graphs. This is a qualification, not validation of Kaal's full substrate. The article concerns research data and provenance. It does not show that settlement, record, and report derive from one base or that an authorized reviewer reconciles them with institutional state.

entry.title: Failed Quality Gate Stops Pipeline Advancement
entry.summary: Gluhak and Pavlič provide direct operational support for Kaal's fail-closed control rule. Their CI/CD case study uses dependent quality checks. If any check fails, the pipeline fails and the code is not integrated into the larger codebase. This independently instantiates a failed control stopping advancement instead of merely annotating a run. The comparison is bounded. The source concerns software-delivery pipelines and static source-code quality, not autonomous-agent reputation infrastructure or Kaal's broader control taxonomy.

entry.title: Machine Learning Run Provenance Reporting Qualification
entry.summary: Samuel, Löffler, and König-Ries provide independent support for the run-level part of Kaal's reporting-layer design. Their study identifies code, data, parameters, package versions, preprocessing, and execution context as information needed to reproduce machine-learning experiments. ProvBook captures, stores, describes, and compares provenance across Jupyter executions. It also binds each model run to its execution environment. This supports preserving run evidence and controls and comparing results across runs. The comparison is bounded. The source concerns machine-learning research pipelines, not autonomous-agent reputation pools, and it does not test periodic institutional summaries. It therefore qualifies the run-level and cross-run provenance components of Kaal's three-part reporting design rather than validating the complete architecture.

entry.summary: Ahn, Isaac, and Salmon provide independent experimental evidence for the design transition in Kaal's evolution-stage claim. The formation rules significantly affect group size, contribution dynamics, and earnings. This supports introducing endogenous formation when testing an institutional arc because fixed membership can suppress behavior generated by formation rules. The comparison is bounded. The source studies human membership in public-goods groups, not autonomous agents forming work, and does not test Kaal's reputation, validation, staking, or three-stage substrate. It therefore qualifies the necessity and implementation level of Kaal's evolution stage rather than validating the architecture.
